paras.text: Policy Interpretation, Audio Lecture

This is the chapter that decides every other chapter. Before you can argue a deadline, a bad faith claim, or an appraisal fight, you have to know how a Michigan court actually reads the words in the contract. Everything downstream assumes you already know this.

And there is a particular reason this chapter is worth slowing down for. Most of what you will hear on a job site about what a policy means is wrong, confidently. The homeowner has a theory, the adjuster has a theory, and the contractor has a theory, and Michigan law agrees with almost none of them. What I am going to give you is the actual order of operations a court uses.
Eleven ideas, in the order Michigan courts apply them. After most of them I will ask you a question and then go quiet. Answer out loud.
Idea one. Rory, and the sentence that ends most arguments.

The single most important rule in Michigan insurance law comes from Rory versus Continental Insurance Company, Michigan Supreme Court, July twenty eighth, two thousand five. The dispute itself was small, a one year deadline to sue under an auto policy, but the holding reaches every policy in the state.
Unambiguous contracts, including insurance policies, are enforced as written unless a provision violates a law or public policy.

Then the court went further, and this second half is the part that does the work. Judicial determinations of reasonableness are an invalid basis to refuse to enforce an unambiguous contract provision.

Sit with what that means. A judge cannot look at a clear policy term, decide it seems unfair, and rewrite it. Before Rory, lower courts had been using exactly that door, striking policy language they considered unreasonable. Rory shut it.
So if you remember one sentence from this chapter, make it this one. Unambiguous language wins, and fairness is not a legal argument.
That is a hard thing to say to a homeowner standing in a burned kitchen. It is still the law.
Idea two. Wilkie, and a doctrine Michigan threw out.
This one matters because other states do have it, and if you read national material you will absorb it by accident.

In some states an insured can argue that even though the policy says one thing, a reasonable policyholder expected something broader, and the court should honor that expectation instead of the words on the page. That is the reasonable expectations doctrine.

Michigan does not have it. Wilkie versus Auto Owners Insurance Company, Michigan Supreme Court, July sixteenth, two thousand three, held flatly that the rule of reasonable expectations has no application in Michigan, and overruled the prior cases that had recognized it.

So when a homeowner says, I always assumed my policy covered this, hear that for what it is. Sympathetic, sometimes genuinely sad, and not a legal theory in Michigan. It does not move an unambiguous exclusion an inch.
Question. Homeowner says the policy is unfair and that nobody would have expected this exclusion. Name the two cases that dispose of both halves of that, and what each one says.

Rory, two thousand five, unambiguous provisions are enforced as written and a judge cannot refuse on reasonableness grounds. Wilkie, two thousand three, the reasonable expectations doctrine has no application in Michigan.
Idea three. Klapp, ambiguity, and the order of operations everybody gets wrong.

If reasonable expectations does not work, what does an insured do when the policy language genuinely conflicts with itself? That is Klapp versus United Insurance Group Agency, Michigan Supreme Court, June eighteenth, two thousand three.

Memorize this citation, because it gets mangled constantly. Four hundred sixty eight Michigan four hundred fifty nine. Not four sixteen. Four fifty nine. Hear that pair, because the wrong number is the one people repeat.

Klapp defines ambiguity this way. A contract is ambiguous when its provisions are capable of conflicting interpretations. If two clauses in the same policy irreconcilably conflict, the policy is ambiguous.
Now here is the part almost everybody gets wrong, including people who cite this case for a living. Finding an ambiguity does not mean the insured wins.

Klapp sets an order of operations. First the factfinder looks at extrinsic evidence, meaning things outside the four corners of the policy. The application. Correspondence with the agent. Industry custom. Anything showing what the parties actually intended.
And if that evidence answers the question, that answer controls, even if it favors the insurance company.

Only after all of that fails does contra proferentem apply, the rule that ambiguous language is construed against whoever drafted it, which is almost always the insurer. Klapp calls contra proferentem a tie breaker, used only after conventional interpretation, including extrinsic evidence, has been tried and found wanting.

So the trap answer is: I found an ambiguity, therefore the insured wins. The real answer is: I found an ambiguity, therefore we go look at extrinsic evidence, and only if that comes up empty does the insured get the benefit of the tie breaker.
Question. You find two clauses in a policy that irreconcilably conflict. What happens next, and what does not happen next.

What happens next is extrinsic evidence, the application, agent correspondence, industry custom, to find what the parties actually intended, and that controls even if it helps the carrier. What does not happen is the insured automatically winning. Contra proferentem is a last resort tie breaker.
Idea four. Who proves what. A two step relay race.

Step one belongs to the insured. Heniser versus Frankenmuth Mutual Insurance Company, Michigan Supreme Court, July sixth, nineteen ninety five, holds that it is the insured's burden to establish that the claim falls within the terms of the policy.
Step two comes only after step one is satisfied: whether that coverage is negated by an exclusion.

Now read Heniser carefully, because this is where a lot of study material goes wrong. Heniser gives you the order, and the insured's half of the burden, and nothing more. It never says the insurer carries the burden on the exclusion.

For that half you cite a different case. Hunt versus Drielick, four hundred ninety six Michigan three hundred sixty six, two thousand fourteen. Hunt restates Heniser's test and then quotes an older case, Fresard, for the rule that the insurer should bear the burden of proving an absence of coverage.
Hunt also adds the counterweights, and they cut both ways. Exclusionary clauses are strictly construed in favor of the insured. But clear and specific exclusions must be enforced.
So the pair is: Heniser for step one, Hunt for step two. Two cases, two halves. If somebody cites Heniser for the insurer's burden, they have overstated it.
And the practical consequence is worth saying plainly. If the carrier cannot prove the exclusion fits the facts, the insured's initial showing of coverage stands and the claim is owed.
Question. Which case gives you the insured's burden, which gives you the insurer's, and what is the mistake people make.

Heniser, nineteen ninety five, the insured proves the claim falls within the policy. Hunt versus Drielick, two thousand fourteen, the insurer bears the burden of proving an absence of coverage. The mistake is citing Heniser for both halves. It only does the first.
Idea five. An honest gap, and why I am telling you about it.

Here is a question that comes up in almost every real dispute. Suppose the insurer proves an exclusion applies, but that exclusion has its own exception, something like an ensuing loss clause. Whose burden is the exception?
Logically it should be the insured's, since the insured is the one who benefits from it. But no controlling Michigan case squarely holding that was opened this session.

So know the logic, and do not quote a Michigan case name for it. If you attach a case name to a proposition that case does not hold, you will get caught, and everything else you said gets doubted with it. Being able to say I know the reasoning and I do not have Michigan authority for it is a stronger position than a confident wrong cite.
Idea six. Kirschner, and the word usually.

This is where insureds try to argue their way into coverage that was never sold to them. Kirschner versus Process Design Associates, Michigan Supreme Court, May eleventh, nineteen ninety nine, is the controlling case.
The key word is usually, and you should notice it every single time you see this case cited.

Kirschner holds that the application of waiver and estoppel is limited, and usually the doctrines will not be applied to broaden coverage to protect the insured against risks that were not included in the policy or that were expressly excluded.
Why not? The court's own reason is the memorable part. An insurance company should not be required to pay for a loss for which it has charged no premium.
That is the whole logic in one line. You cannot get coverage for free just because someone at the insurance company said something careless on the phone.

But usually is not never, and the exam of real life will hand you the exception. Kirschner points to two situations where courts have let waiver or estoppel work. Where the insurance company misrepresented the terms of the policy. And where the insurer defended the insured in a liability case without reserving the right to later deny coverage.

Even then it takes a showing that the inequity to the insured outweighs the inequity to the insurer. And note this, because it tells you how narrow the opening is: Kirschner applied neither exception on its own facts.

Outside those two patterns, a verbal assurance from an adjuster almost never survives. Which is exactly why you get coverage commitments in writing. If an adjuster says do not worry, we will cover the detached garage, and there is no endorsement for it, that promise is not enough on its own.
Question. Adjuster tells your homeowner on the phone that the detached garage is covered. It is not in the policy. What are the two Kirschner openings, and does a phone call fit either.

The two openings are the insurer misrepresenting the terms of the policy, and the insurer defending a liability case without a reservation of rights. A casual phone assurance is neither, and you would still have to show the inequity to the insured outweighs the inequity to the insurer.
Idea seven. Salesin, overhead and profit, and the trap on both sides.
This is where restoration contractors and public adjusters spend a lot of energy, so let me give you both the win and the limit.
The case is Salesin versus State Farm Fire and Casualty Company, Michigan Court of Appeals, April twenty first, nineteen ninety eight, published.
Salesin repaired his own home instead of hiring a general contractor. State Farm argued that since he never actually paid a contractor's overhead and profit, he should not be paid for it.

The court rejected that. Not actually incurring the cost is, in its words, not dispositive. It adopted a test from a Pennsylvania case, Gilderman: repair or replacement costs include any cost the insured is reasonably likely to incur, and in some instances that includes a general contractor and his twenty percent overhead and profit.

Now the trap, and it runs the other direction from what contractors want. Salesin does not create an automatic rule that overhead and profit is always owed. The court said so directly. Gilderman does not support the position that overhead and profit should always and automatically be included in an actual cash value payment.
So what is the actual test? Whether a general contractor was reasonably likely to be needed for that scope. Not whether one was hired.

Picture the two ends of it. A single trade repair, say just replacing carpet, is a weak case. Nobody is reasonably likely to need a general contractor to coordinate one flooring crew. Now a multi trade rebuild, roofing, drywall, flooring, and paint in sequence, is exactly the situation Gilderman and Salesin describe, where a homeowner is reasonably likely to need someone coordinating trades. There, overhead and profit belongs in the payment regardless of who swings the hammer.
Match the argument to the scope of work, not to a blanket rule. A blanket rule is how you lose an argument you should have won.
Question. Homeowner does the work himself on a four trade rebuild and the carrier strips overhead and profit because he hired nobody. What is your answer, and what is the answer you should not give.

The answer is Salesin: not incurring the cost is not dispositive, and the test is whether a general contractor was reasonably likely to be needed, which on a four trade sequence it is. The answer you should not give is that overhead and profit is always owed, because Salesin expressly says it is not automatic.
Idea eight. When a covered peril and an excluded peril combine.
There are three competing legal tools fighting over this outcome, and you should be able to name all three before you pick one.

Concurrent causation says a covered peril's contribution alone triggers coverage. Efficient proximate cause says the dominant cause that started the chain controls the whole loss. And an anti concurrent causation clause, an A C C clause, is language the insurer writes into the exclusion to shut both doctrines off, by saying the exclusion applies regardless of any other cause, whether it acted before, during, or after the excluded peril.
Michigan's controlling authority is Sunshine Motors Incorporated versus New Hampshire Insurance Company, Michigan Court of Appeals, February twenty second, nineteen ninety five, published.

Here are the facts, because they are easy to picture. A car dealership flooded when heavy rain combined with a piece of wood partially blocking the local drainage system. The insured argued the blocked drain was a separate, non excluded cause.

The court disagreed, and the reason is entirely about the policy language. The exclusion carried exactly the anti concurrent causation wording I just described: coverage excluded regardless of any other cause or event contributing concurrently or in any sequence to the loss. So whether the blocked drain was a direct or an indirect cause, the principal factor or merely a contributing factor, made no difference. The policy expressly excluded coverage either way.
Now let me be honest about the limits, because overselling this is how people lose credibility. Sunshine Motors is a Court of Appeals decision and it is carrier favorable.

But the Supreme Court has spoken on the underlying doctrine and went the same direction. In Vanguard Insurance Company versus Clarke, four hundred thirty eight Michigan four hundred sixty three, nineteen ninety one, a Court of Appeals panel used what the Supreme Court called the minority rule of concurrent causation to defeat an auto related exclusion in a homeowner's liability policy. The Supreme Court reversed, saying it discerned no compelling legal or policy basis for that doctrine to nullify an unambiguous exclusion.

Vanguard is a liability case, not a first party property case, so do not oversell it either. But between the two, no Michigan case adopting a broad, pro coverage concurrent causation doctrine, the way Florida's Sebo decision did, was found this session.

One argument does survive, and it is the practical one. You can try to segregate damage caused solely by the covered peril. That rests on the exclusion's own caused by wording, not on any Michigan case found this run, so do not claim a Michigan court has blessed it.
Idea nine. Direct physical loss, and a case that is widely misquoted.
You will see this phrase in almost every business income and civil authority form: direct physical loss of or damage to property.

Michigan's leading statement on it came out of the COVID nineteen wave. Gavrilides Management Company versus Michigan Insurance Company, Michigan Court of Appeals docket number three five four four one eight, published February first, twenty twenty two.
Two Lansing area restaurants were closed by the governor's pandemic orders and sought business income coverage, arguing the closure itself was a direct physical loss.

The court disagreed, and here is its actual language, because a wrong paraphrase of this case circulates widely. The word physical necessarily requires the loss or damage to have some manner of tangible and measurable presence or effect in, on, or to the premises. The restaurants, it said, were unambiguously closed by impersonal operation of a general law, not because anything about or inside the premises had physically changed.

Now the part people get backwards, and it is the reason to be careful with this case. Gavrilides did not stop at the coverage trigger. The plaintiffs asked to amend to allege the virus was physically present, so the court said it was necessary to address that alternative basis for denying coverage, and in a separate section held that the defendant properly denied the claim pursuant to the virus exclusion.
Two holdings, not one. If you cite Gavrilides for only the first, somebody who has read it will correct you.

And the lesson generalizes far beyond COVID, which is why it belongs in a property chapter at all. Direct physical loss requires something tangible and measurable in, on, or to the premises. A legal restriction on how the property may be used, without more, does not meet that bar in Michigan.
Idea ten. Actual cash value, the statutory floor, and the depreciation fight.

Michigan Compiled Laws section five hundred point twenty eight thirty three, subsection one, paragraph a, sets a statutory floor. Every fire insurance policy in Michigan must provide, at a minimum, coverage for the actual cash value of the property at the time of the loss.
Now notice what it does not do. It sets a floor and never defines how actual cash value is calculated. That gap is the whole fight.
The Department of Insurance and Financial Services, D I F S, addressed that gap in Bulletin twenty twenty four dash twenty six dash I N S, issued November eighth, twenty twenty four.
The bulletin describes actual cash value as ordinarily meaning the loss of value due to wear and tear, deterioration, and obsolescence to physical or tangible items.

Then it makes the key move. Nontangible items, defined as labor, taxes, fees, and overhead and profit, are not physical objects, and do not deteriorate, age, or decline in value the way a roof or a carpet does.

Hear the logic there, because it is genuinely good. You can depreciate a twenty year old roof because the shingles wore out. You cannot depreciate the labor of installing it, because labor does not sit on a roof getting older.

Now the trap, and it is a trap in the direction of overclaiming. For personal lines homeowners or dwelling policies issued or renewed effective July first, twenty twenty five or after, an insurer that wants to depreciate a nontangible item in an actual cash value payment can only do so through a standalone endorsement identifying those items, not by burying it in the policy form's definitions. That endorsement has to be optional, and because it reduces coverage, it has to be offered with a commensurate premium reduction.

What the bulletin does not do is ban depreciating labor, taxes, fees, or overhead and profit. It conditions the practice on transparency. Those are very different things, and the difference is the whole argument.

And remember the instrument hierarchy from chapter one. A bulletin is guidance from the D I F S director, not a statute. Proof of that: D I F S superseded an earlier bulletin, twenty twenty four dash eighteen dash I N S, through that same administrative process, with no legislative vote required. What one bulletin gives, another can take.

Question. Carrier depreciates labor on a claim under a policy renewed in September twenty twenty five, with nothing but a definition buried in the form. What is wrong, and what is the thing you must not say.

It needed a standalone, optional endorsement identifying those nontangible items, offered with a commensurate premium reduction, not a buried definition. What you must not say is that depreciating labor is banned. The bulletin conditions it on transparency, and it is a bulletin, not a statute.
Idea eleven. Named peril versus open peril.
This last one is industry background rather than Michigan law, but it decides which side is even arguing.

A named peril policy lists the perils it covers, and anything left off the list is not covered. An open peril policy, sometimes called special form or all risk, covers everything except what is specifically excluded.
You already saw that grant quoted inside Gavrilides: covered causes of loss means risks of direct physical loss, unless excluded or limited.

And the common H O three form splits the difference, which is why homeowners get confused about their own policy. Dwelling and other structures are open peril. Personal property is typically named peril unless the homeowner upgrades.

So on the same policy, the building is covered unless the carrier finds an exclusion, and the contents are covered only if the cause is on the list. That single split explains a large share of the arguments you will have over a contents claim.
Time for the rapid fire recap. I am going to say these fast. You are not learning them now, you are checking which ones you already have.

Rory, two thousand five: unambiguous contracts enforced as written, no judicial reasonableness override. Wilkie, two thousand three: no reasonable expectations doctrine in Michigan. Klapp, four sixty eight Michigan four fifty nine, two thousand three: contra proferentem is a last resort tie breaker, after extrinsic evidence. Heniser, nineteen ninety five: insured proves coverage first. Hunt versus Drielick, two thousand fourteen: insurer proves the absence of coverage. Kirschner, nineteen ninety nine: waiver and estoppel usually will not broaden coverage. Salesin, nineteen ninety eight: self performance is not dispositive on overhead and profit, but there is no automatic rule. Sunshine Motors, nineteen ninety five: anti concurrent causation clauses are enforced where they actually appear in the exclusion at issue. Vanguard, nineteen ninety one: the Supreme Court will not let concurrent causation nullify an unambiguous exclusion. Gavrilides, twenty twenty two: direct physical loss needs something tangible and measurable in, on, or to the premises, and that same opinion separately enforced the virus exclusion. Bulletin twenty twenty four dash twenty six dash I N S: a standalone, optional, premium reduced endorsement before an insurer depreciates labor, taxes, fees, or overhead and profit, on policies issued or renewed on or after July first, twenty twenty five.
Learn this chapter cold, because every other chapter in this track assumes you already know how Michigan reads a policy. If any of the questions I asked gave you trouble, that is where to drill.
